title: Alexander Morus: honest civil acts are possible in the state of sin
source_text: IV. Neque ab his abludit quod docet Alexander Morus, bona moralia absolute spectata ab homine in statu peccati perfici posse. Potest enim, inquit, quivis caste sobrieque vivere quoad actus externos, manus a furto & homicidio abstinere, locomotivam regere, coetibus Ecclesiae interesse, Evangelium audire libenter, non instar surdae aspidis aures obturare: quae omnia honesta sunt & civilia, Deoque minus ingrata quando utcunque usurpantur, quam ubi profana contemptione omittuntur. De Victoria gratiae disputatione secunda, Thesi 41.
pass_a_gloss: IV. Nor from these does it differ what Alexander Morus teaches, that moral goods absolutely regarded by man in the state of sin can be performed. For any one can, he says, live chastely and soberly as to external acts, keep the hands from theft and homicide, govern the locomotive power, be present at the assemblies of the Church, hear the Gospel willingly, not like the deaf adder stop the ears: all which are honest and civil, and less unwelcome to God when they are in any way practised, than where with profane contempt they are omitted. On the Victory of grace disputation second, Thesis 41.
pass_b_english: Thesis IV. Nor is this far from what Alexander Morus teaches: that moral goods, taken absolutely, can be performed by man in the state of sin. 'Anyone can,' he says, 'live chastely and soberly as far as outward acts go, keep his hands from theft and murder, govern his power of movement, attend the gatherings of the Church, and hear the Gospel gladly instead of stopping his ears like the deaf adder.

All these things are upright and civil, and God finds them less displeasing when they are practised in whatever way than when they are left undone out of profane contempt' (On the Victory of Grace, second disputation, thesis 41).

lemmas.latin: non instar surdae aspidis aures obturare
lemmas.gloss: not like the deaf adder stop the ears

choices.why: Melanchthon's term (Apology, art. 18) for the outward uprightness of which reason is capable; 'righteousness' keeps the link with justitia elsewhere in the treatise.
